subject: Biology
description: Bacteria — structure, classification (Gram +/-), reproduction, useful and harmful bacteria, antibiotics, diseases, fermentation roles.

questions.stem: Bacteria are classified as PROKARYOTES because they:
questions.explanation: PROKARYOTES (bacteria + archaea) lack a TRUE NUCLEUS — their DNA floats freely in the CYTOPLASM as a single circular CHROMOSOME called a NUCLEOID. They also LACK membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, no ER, no Golgi, no lysosomes). EUKARYOTES (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a NUCLEUS bounded by a NUCLEAR MEMBRANE + multiple membrane-bound organelles. KEY BACTERIAL FEATURES: (1) Cell wall of PEPTIDOGLYCAN (target of penicillin antibiotics). (2) Reproduce by BINARY FISSION (asexual; very fast — E. coli divides every 20 minutes under good conditions). (3) Some have FLAGELLA for motility. (4) Many have EXTRA-chromosomal DNA called PLASMIDS — carry antibiotic-resistance genes; basis of biotechnology. SIZE: ~1-2 micrometres (μm); ~10× smaller than a typical animal cell. NUMBER: human gut has ~10¹⁴ bacteria — outnumbering our own cells! NCERT CLASS 11, CH. 2 — top biology MCQ topic.

questions.stem: Which of these diseases is caused by BACTERIA?

options.option_text: Influenza caused by an RNA virus

questions.explanation: TUBERCULOSIS (TB) is caused by MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS, discovered by Robert Koch (1882) — Nobel Prize 1905. INDIA TB STATS: world's highest TB burden — ~28% of global TB cases. India aims to ELIMINATE TB by 2025 (Modi govt commitment, vs WHO 2030 target). DIAGNOSIS: sputum microscopy, GeneXpert (rapid PCR), Mantoux skin test. TREATMENT: 6-month DOTS regimen (Directly Observed Treatment Short-course); resistance growing — MDR-TB and XDR-TB are global concerns. OTHER MAJOR BACTERIAL DISEASES: cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella), tetanus (Clostridium tetani), diphtheria (Corynebacterium), pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae), leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae), plague (Yersinia pestis), gonorrhoea (Neisseria), syphilis (Treponema pallidum). VACCINE: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) — given at birth in India for TB protection. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 disease-by-causative-agent Qs per CGL, NEET, IBPS GA section.

questions.stem: Which bacterium is responsible for converting milk to curd through fermentation?
questions.explanation: LACTOBACILLUS bacteria convert milk's LACTOSE (sugar) into LACTIC ACID, which curdles milk proteins (casein) into the gel-like network we call curd/yoghurt. PROCESS: milk warmed to ~40°C, inoculated with starter culture (live curd or commercial starter), kept warm 4-6 hours. INDIA: 'dahi' is a daily staple; ~30% of household milk consumption goes to curd-making. PROBIOTICS: Lactobacillus is beneficial gut flora — many curd brands (Yakult, Mother Dairy probio) market this benefit. OTHER FERMENTATION BACTERIA: (1) Streptococcus thermophilus — also in yoghurt. (2) Lactobacillus delbrueckii — Bulgarian yoghurt. (3) Acetobacter — vinegar production from ethanol. (4) Propionibacterium — Swiss cheese (creates the holes via CO₂). USEFUL BACTERIA: Rhizobium (nitrogen-fixation in legume roots), E. coli (gut, also lab workhorse), Streptomyces (source of streptomycin antibiotic). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'curd-bacteria = Lactobacillus' is a Class 8 NCERT staple, tested in CGL/IBPS Clerk every cycle.

questions.explanation: BINARY FISSION: a single bacterial cell DUPLICATES its DNA, the cytoplasm divides, and the cell splits into TWO IDENTICAL daughters. SPEED: under ideal conditions (warmth, food, moisture), E. coli divides every 20 MINUTES — meaning 1 cell becomes ~10⁹ cells in just 10 hours (theoretical, before nutrients deplete). NOT MITOSIS: mitosis requires a NUCLEAR MEMBRANE that prokaryotes lack. NOT MEIOSIS: bacteria don't produce gametes; they're not sexually reproducing in the eukaryotic sense. SUPPLEMENTARY MECHANISMS for genetic variation in bacteria: (1) CONJUGATION — DNA transfer via PILI (sexual-like process). (2) TRANSFORMATION — uptake of free DNA from environment (Griffith's classic experiment, 1928). (3) TRANSDUCTION — DNA transferred via bacteriophage (virus). These processes spread ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE — a major global health concern. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'binary fission' is a JEE-NEET, SSC, RRB Group D MCQ — appears 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests prokaryote-vs-eukaryote reproduction distinction.

questions.stem: Which bacterium fixes atmospheric NITROGEN in legume root nodules?

options.option_text: E. coli is gut bacterium only.

questions.explanation: RHIZOBIUM lives symbiotically in the root nodules of LEGUMES (peas, beans, soybeans, lentils, peanuts, gram, lucerne). It converts atmospheric N₂ into AMMONIA (NH₃) via the NITROGENASE enzyme — a process called BIOLOGICAL NITROGEN FIXATION. The plant gives Rhizobium sugars (photosynthates); Rhizobium gives the plant usable nitrogen — classic mutualism. AGRICULTURAL IMPACT: this is why CROP ROTATION with legumes (e.g., wheat-soybean-wheat) restores soil nitrogen naturally — saving fertilizer costs. INDIA traditional cropping: pulses (dal) are routinely intercropped with cereals for this reason. OTHER N-FIXERS: Azotobacter (free-living in soil), Anabaena and Nostoc (cyanobacteria, fix N in rice paddy water — Azolla-Anabaena symbiosis), Frankia (in non-legume root nodules — alder, Casuarina). NITROGEN CYCLE: N₂ → NH₃ (fixation) → NO₃⁻ (nitrification by Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) → plant uptake → death/decay → ammonification → back to N₂ (denitrification). PYQ FREQUENCY: top biology+agriculture MCQ — 1-2 per CGL/NEET cycle.

questions.stem: GRAM-POSITIVE bacteria differ from Gram-negative bacteria in that they have:

options.option_text: No cell wall at all alone

questions.explanation: GRAM STAIN test (developed by Hans Christian Gram, 1884) classifies bacteria by their CELL WALL structure: GRAM-POSITIVE (purple after stain): THICK peptidoglycan layer (~20-80 nm thick, multiple layers) — retains crystal violet dye. Examples: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Bacillus, Clostridium, Lactobacillus. GRAM-NEGATIVE (pink after stain): THIN peptidoglycan (~7-8 nm, single layer) PLUS an OUTER MEMBRANE with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) — doesn't retain crystal violet but takes up safranin counter-stain (pink). Examples: E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, Vibrio cholerae, Neisseria, Helicobacter pylori. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Gram status determines ANTIBIOTIC choice — penicillins target peptidoglycan synthesis (more effective on Gram-positive); Gram-negatives have outer membrane that BLOCKS many drugs. LPS in Gram-negatives is an ENDOTOXIN — causes septic shock during severe infection. NCERT BIO Class 11 covers this; routinely tested in NEET 1× per cycle. EXAM-FAVORITE: cell-wall structure determines drug efficacy.

questions.stem: Which scientist is known as the FATHER of modern microbiology for proving that bacteria cause disease?
questions.explanation: LOUIS PASTEUR (1822-1895, France) — the FATHER OF MODERN MICROBIOLOGY. Major contributions: (1) GERM THEORY OF DISEASE (1860s) — proved diseases are caused by microorganisms, not 'bad air' (miasma). (2) PASTEURIZATION — heating beverages to kill bacteria (still used for milk today). (3) RABIES VACCINE (1885) — first vaccinated 9-year-old Joseph Meister; saved his life from rabies. (4) ANTHRAX VACCINE for sheep (1881) — public-demonstration showcase. (5) Disproved SPONTANEOUS GENERATION (microbes don't arise from nothing) using his classic SWAN-NECK FLASK experiment. ROBERT KOCH (German, 1843-1910, Nobel 1905) — also founder of medical microbiology; identified TB and cholera bacteria; Koch's postulates (criteria for proving causation). PASTEUR vs KOCH: Pasteur was process-oriented (vaccines, fermentation); Koch was identification-oriented (which microbe causes which disease). NOBEL connection: Pasteur died before Nobels began (1901). PYQ ANGLE: 'Pasteur germ theory' top-3 history-of-science MCQ in NEET, SSC.
